images.filename: Richard Rowland Kirkland Monument in the Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park.jpg
images.caption: Monument honoring Richard Rowland Kirkland in the Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park honoring his bravery and humanitarian actions during the Battle of Fredericksburg. The monument was crafted by Felix de Weldon (dedicated 1965) and was placed on land previously owned by Mary Washington College. The land was later transferred to the National Park Service in 1987. The inscription says: "In memoriam / Richard Rowland Kirkland / Co. G, 2nd South Carolina Volunteers / C. S. A. / At the risk of his life, this American / soldier of sublime compassion brought / water to his wounded foes at / Fredericksburg. The fighting men on / both sides of the line called him / 'The Angel of Marye's Heights'".

images.filename: Fifth Corps Monument in Fredericksburg National Cemetery.jpg
images.caption:
The Fifth Corps Monument in the Fredericksburg National Cemetery. The monument was dedicated in 1901 and was erected largely through the efforts of Daniel Butterfield, the V Corps commander for the Battle of Fredericksburg. August 2010.
The inscription on the monument reads as follows:
"To Commemorate the Valor
of
The Fifth Corps
Army of the Potomac
and
In Loving Memory of
Its Heroic Dead

This Monument has been Erected by
Major General
Daniel Butterfield U.S.V.
Its Commander on the Field

December 13 1862"

images.filename: Parker's Battery Memorial in Fredericksburg National Cemetery.jpg
images.caption: The Parker's Battery Memorial is located in the Fredericksburg National Cemetery. The memorial honors the men of Captain William Parker's Virginia Battery which was defeated on Marye's Heights 3 May 1893 during the Second Battle of Fredericksburg.
images.alt: The Parker's Battery Memorial is located in the Fredericksburg National Cemetery. The memorial honors the men of Captain William Parker's Virginia Battery which was defeated on Marye's Heights 3 May 1893 during the Second Battle of Fredericksburg.

images.filename: Innis House Exterior and Sunken Road in Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park.jpg
images.caption: Exterior view of the Innis House. Located along Sunken Road, the Innis House is closest to the intersection of the modern Mercer and Willis Streets in Fredericksburg. The Innis House was used as a firing position by Confederate sharp shooters during the Battle of Fredericksburg. The Innis House was a private residence until the 1970's when it was sold to the park and the exterior was restored to its 1962 appearance. The section of stone wall in front of the Innis House was restored in 2004.
images.alt: Exterior view of the Innis House. Located along Sunken Road, the Innis House is closest to the intersection of the modern Mercer and Willis Streets in Fredericksburg. images.filename: Innis House Interior in Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park.jpg
images.caption: Interior view of the Innis House and the original damage sustained during the Battle of Fredericksburg. The Innis House was built around 1861 and owned by Martha Stephens, John Innis lived in the house in 1861. The home was lived in through 1970 when it was sold to the National Park Service, during restoration layers of wall board and wallpaper were removed revealing the original 1862 damage.
images.alt: Interior view of the Innis House and the original damage sustained during the Battle of Fredericksburg. images.filename: Sunken Road Original Section in Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park.jpg
images.caption: The only remaining original section of the Sunken Road's stone wall in the Fredericksburg and Spotsylvania National Military Park. The  Kirkland Monument can be seen on the far side of the wall, while Marye's Heights is to the left of the road. The modern road of Hanover Street can be seen at the end of the Sunken Road.
